Text: "non-experts rate AI stories with 1.19 more points (t = 12.76, p < .001)". corrections.source_says: Keep the non-expert outcome at 273 stories, using the median of five ratings per story from the independent sample of 96 judges. Move the LLM creativity results to a separate automated_score outcome with n_units=431 and the mean of three LLM judges. The existing LLM means, SDs and test statistic are accurate; they describe the full corpus, not the non-expert subset.
corrections.quote: We also prompt three LLMs, i.e. Claude, Gemini and GPT-4, to rate each of the 431 stories on the same five variables.
corrections.locator: PDF p. 5, Human Non-expert Judges and LLM Judges; p. 7, Who’s more creative according to our judges?; p. 8, Table 2.

corrections.form_value: Only S1-O1 through S1-O5 are listed; notes is empty. Originality, surprise and effectiveness ratings are absent, and thematic diversity and complexity outcomes are not recorded.
corrections.source_says: Table 2 reports originality, surprise and effectiveness separately for expert, non-expert and LLM judges, in addition to creativity. The paper also scores lexical n-gram diversity, theme counts, and lexical/syntactic complexity; lexical diversity is only mentioned inside the embedding-based S1-O1 entry. Make the different measures distinguishable, record the main outcomes up to the form’s 15-outcome limit, and identify all omitted measures in notes. The quote gives the missing Table 2 rows in the printed column order: expert Human/AI, non-expert Human/AI, LLM Human/AI.
corrections.locator: PDF p. 8, Table 2 and Figure 8; p. 3, Figure 2a; pp. 4-6, Diversity and Complexity methods/results; pp. 18-19, Figures 9-10. Form-spec.md, rule 7.

corrections.source_says: Populate metric as inverse homogenization (mean pairwise semantic distance), embedding_model as gte-large, and computed_over as each story against all other stories written on the same item set, using 1 − cosine similarity. The definition does not explicitly restrict the reference set to the same creator group. The uncertainty method behind the reported automated-metric p-value is not stated; do not infer a bootstrap, permutation, or independent-pair test.

confirmed: The local full text is arXiv:2411.02316v5 [cs.CL], dated 10 May 2025, with 23 PDF pages; the title and authors match the form (PDF p. 1 and document page count). The whole markdown, including references and appendices, was read.

The study compares independently generated human and model stories; it contains no random assignment of people to generative-AI assistance. design_class=ai_vs_human, context_class=ai_vs_human and core=no are correct (PDF pp. 1 and 3, Figure 1 and Story Generation Data Collection).

The paper reports 60 recruited writers and 59 remaining after instruction-related exclusions, not a randomized sample. These writers exceed the 50-person threshold; the independent judges are not additional writers (PDF p. 3, Story Generation Data Collection; p. 5, judge samples).

The UK Prolific writer sample, 43% female and mean age 38.8, is stated. The paper reports 60 different models, prompted zero-shot with temperature=0.7 and top_p=0.95; the named model examples occur in the model list (PDF p. 3; pp. 14-15, Tables 6-7).

Four three-word item sets and a maximum-five-sentence instruction are stated. The reported 480 collected stories become 431 after removing stories shorter than 3 or longer than 7 sentences; Table 10 prints totals of 208 human and 223 AI stories (PDF p. 3; p. 23, Table 10).

Two expert judges score all 431 valid stories and their scores are averaged; 96 non-expert judges supply five ratings per story for 273 stories, aggregated by the paper’s stated median rule; three LLM judges rate all 431 stories (PDF p. 5, Story Evaluation by Judges).

S1-O1’s p < 0.0001 for higher human lexical/semantic diversity, S1-O2’s novelty thresholds p < 0.01, p < 0.1, p < 0.05 and p < 0.05, and S1-O3’s p < 0.001 for surprise match the PDF exactly (PDF p. 5, Diversity; p. 6, Novelty and Surprise; Figures 2-4).
Expert creativity: Human 3.58 (±0.78), AI 2.33 (±0.55); the prose gives 1.25 points, t = −19.34, p < .001. All match S1-O4 and the one-line finding (PDF p. 7; p. 8, Table 2).

Non-expert creativity: Human 2.45 (±0.77), AI 3.65 (±0.78); the prose explicitly gives 1.19 points, t = 12.76, p < .001. Retain the printed 1.19 rather than replacing it with a difference calculated from rounded means (PDF p. 7; p. 8, Table 2).

LLM creativity: Human 2.41 (±0.70), AI 4.26 (±0.64); the prose gives 1.85 points, t = 28.75, p < .001. These numerical values and the direction in the one-line finding are correct (PDF p. 7; p. 8, Table 2).

The supplementary tables and figures are included on PDF pp. 13-23. Study materials are linked at https://github.com/mismayil/creative-story-gen (PDF p. 9, Ethics and footnote 2); appendix automated-metric figures do not print numerical standard errors or test statistics.

This is an original empirical comparison, not a synthesis; there are no pooled study estimates or standardizers to record. Table 3 predicts judge ratings from story metrics and does not estimate an effect of human AI assistance (PDF pp. 3-8, Methods and Results).
summary: The paper is correctly classified as AI-versus-human context evidence, with 59 retained writers and no randomized human AI-assistance study. The reported numbers match the PDF, but separate LLM rating outcomes, omitted measures, and incomplete or misleading coding fields need correction.
